title: The Forgotten Desirable Difficulty - Reduced Feedback
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner argues that of the Bjorks' five 'desirable difficulties,' reduced feedback is the most neglected despite being as powerful as interleaving, spaced practice, and retrieval practice. He opens with the familiar classroom paradox: a student 'flying' through practice with instant correction on every answer seems to be learning, but a week later the same student can't perform the task — because constant feedback creates a 'fluency trap' where smooth performance is mistaken for durable mastery. Kirschner explains that reducing both the frequency and the specificity of feedback forces students to build their own internal monitoring, retrieval, and self-evaluation capacities rather than depending on an external 'corrector' (teacher, app, or answer key). He describes a practical fading sequence — from specific, immediate correction for novices toward general, delayed prompts for more capable learners — and stresses this must be done deliberately in two directions at once (less often, and less detailed) to transfer responsibility for error-detection from teacher to learner. A clearly marked warning tempers the argument: reduced feedback is only 'desirable' once a learner has enough foundational knowledge to plausibly self-correct; withholding it from true novices produces confusion and frustration rather than productive struggle.
points: Kirschner's central mechanism: immediate, constant feedback creates a 'fluency trap' where smooth practice performance is mistaken for durable learning, but the underlying skill evaporates without the external correction.

He distinguishes two independent dimensions of 'reducing' feedback — frequency (how often) and specificity (how detailed) — and argues both should be faded deliberately and simultaneously as learners gain competence.

Delayed feedback forces a distinct, valuable cognitive act he calls 'second order retrieval': the learner must reconstruct their own reasoning process, not just recall the content, before they can evaluate it against the correction.

A hard caveat limits the whole argument: reduced feedback is 'desirable' only for learners with enough foundational knowledge to plausibly self-correct — applied to true novices, it produces confusion and frustration rather than productive struggle.

His practical test for calibration: if learners respond to fading feedback by checking, explaining, and self-correcting, the difficulty is well-judged; if they respond by guessing or repeating the same error, feedback was withdrawn too soon.
quotes: We've all seen it. A student is 'flying' through practice. Every answer gets an instant tick or cross, every misstep corrected on the spot. The lesson feels smooth. Efficient. Productive. And then, a week later, the same student can't do it.

Frequent feedback acts like a Waze or Google Maps: you arrive at the destination, but you couldn't do the route again without the voice telling you what to do next. In classrooms, that voice is the teacher, the answer key, the autocorrecting app, the constant confirmation or correction that makes the work look right in the moment.

When you reduce feedback, something interesting happens. The learner is forced to rely on internal monitoring processes. They have to ask themselves whether their answer is correct or even plausible, whether a step follows logically from the preceding step, whether what they wrote matches the rule or the concept that they have been taught.
A powerful way to avoid that trap is to fade feedback in two directions at once. Over time you give feedback less frequently, but you also make it less detailed and more general.

Reduced feedback is desirable only when learners have enough foundational knowledge to eventually succeed. If you withhold feedback, or make it too general too soon, for a true novice who can't diagnose errors, you don't create productive struggle; you create confusion and frustration.

The best practical test is to watch what happens as you fade. If learners respond by checking, explaining, comparing their work to a standard, and correcting themselves, you're building the right kind of difficulty.
